# Getting started with MiniMax Code: a beginner's guide

> **In short:** MiniMax Code is an AI helper you reach through its website at agent.minimax.io. You'll need an account, and some features may depend on the plan you choose. Check its current details on the official site. Always review what it gives you before you act on it.

Have you heard that AI tools can help with much more than writing code, but you're not sure where to begin? This guide is for you. By the end, you'll have signed in, sent your first everyday request, and learned a simple habit for checking the answers. You don't need any technical background.

## Before you start

- **An internet connection and a web browser** on a computer, tablet, or phone. A larger screen is easier for beginners.
- **A MiniMax account.** You'll create one on the official site during Step 1.
- **About 20 to 30 minutes** for the whole guide. Plan limits and features may change, so look at the official site for current details.

## Step 1 — Open the official site and find the sign-in button

Type **agent.minimax.io** into your browser's address bar and press Enter. Before you go further, make sure the address in the bar matches exactly, because fake sites often look similar. The home page should load, and you'll usually see a button in the top corner or the center of the page that says something like **Sign in**, **Log in**, or **Get started**. Click it. You'll be asked to create an account or sign in with an email address or another option the page shows.

Choose the option that fits you, enter the details it asks for, and follow the confirmation steps. Use a password you don't use anywhere else.

*If it looks different:* the page layout changes often. If you can't see a sign-in button, look for a menu icon (three short lines) in a corner.

You'll know it worked when the site shows a welcome screen or a chat area instead of the sign-in form.

## Step 2 — Find the place where you type your request

Once you're signed in, look for a large text box near the bottom or center of the screen. It may have placeholder text such as "Ask anything" or "Send a message," though yours may read differently. This is where you type. The tool is designed for back-and-forth conversation, so think of it as a patient assistant you can keep talking to.

Click inside the box, and a blinking cursor should appear. Type a single short test sentence, such as "Hello, can you hear me?" and press the send button, which often looks like a paper plane or an arrow. Wait a few seconds for the reply to appear.

*If it looks different:* if you don't see a text box, look for a button labeled "New chat" or a plus sign, then try again. If nothing responds, refresh the page.

You'll know it worked when your message appears on screen and a reply starts to appear below it.

## Step 3 — Send your first everyday request

Now try something that has nothing to do with programming. Everyday planning is a good starting point. Type a request with a few specific details, because the more context you give, the more useful the answer usually is.

💬 Example: "Help me plan five easy weekday dinners for [number] people. Keep each meal under 30 minutes and list the ingredients for each one."

Replace the bracketed part with your own details. Send the message and read the reply slowly. A good answer usually has a clear structure, such as a list or a set of steps.

*If it looks different:* if the reply is too general, that's normal for a first try. Don't worry. Step 4 shows how to improve it.

You'll know it worked when you get a reply that is organized and relates to the details you gave.

## Step 4 — Ask follow-up questions to improve the answer

The first reply is rarely the final one. Treat it as a draft. Type a follow-up message that points to exactly what you want to change. You can ask it to shorten the answer, add something, or change the tone. The tool remembers the earlier part of the same chat, so you don't need to repeat everything.

💬 Example: "Thanks. Make the list vegetarian, and cut it down to three dinners that need no more than five ingredients each."

Send the message and compare the new reply with the first one. If you're not happy with the result, you can simply keep refining. This back-and-forth is the most useful skill you'll practice.

*If it looks different:* if the tool seems to lose track of the conversation, start a new chat and paste in the key details again. Long chats can get confusing, so shorter ones are often easier to follow.

You'll know it worked when the second reply reflects your changes and keeps the parts you liked.

## Step 5 — Try a summary task, and leave out private details

A very practical use is condensing long text. Find a short article, a newsletter, or a message you're allowed to share, and copy a paragraph or two of it. Paste it into the text box, then type your instruction after it. Keep the text you paste free of passwords, bank numbers, medical details, and anything else private, since you should assume anything you share in a chat is sensitive.

💬 Example: "Summarize the text below in five short bullet points for a busy reader. Text: [paste your paragraph here]"

Read the summary next to the original to check that the main points are really there. Summaries can leave things out or change emphasis, so spot-check them.

*If it looks different:* if pasting doesn't work on your device, type a shorter excerpt by hand instead.

You'll know it worked when the reply lists the main points from the text you shared in a shorter form.

## Step 6 — Check the answer before you trust it

This is the most important step. AI tools can produce confident answers that are incorrect, and that's a known limitation of this whole category of technology. Before you act on any answer that involves facts, dates, prices, or health, financial, or legal matters, check it against an official source. You can also ask the tool to show its assumptions so you know what to verify.

💬 Example: "List the three main assumptions behind your last answer, so I can check each one myself."

Read the list and verify the points that matter most. For health, money, or legal decisions, talk to a qualified professional. The tool can explain a topic, but it isn't a substitute for expert advice.

*If it looks different:* if the tool doesn't give a clear list, ask it directly what it's unsure about in its answer.

You'll know it worked when you can point to the specific claims you still need to verify.

## Common mistakes

- **Typing the same vague request and expecting a perfect answer.** Fix it by adding details like who the answer is for, how long it should be, and what format you want.
- **Sharing private information in the chat.** Fix it by removing names, account numbers, passwords, and personal health details before you paste anything.
- **Trusting every answer without checking.** Fix it by verifying important facts on an official source, as described in Step 6.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** you can use it to plan meals, draft a polite message to a neighbor, or break a long to-do list into smaller steps.
- **For your business or work:** you can use it to outline a presentation, rewrite a meeting summary, or brainstorm ideas, then review the results yourself.
- **If you're just getting started:** begin with low-stakes tasks like planning or summarizing, and build from there.

It can draft, organize, and explain, but it can't confirm that what it says is true, and it can't see your files, email, or accounts unless you share the content in the chat.

## Try it now

Open agent.minimax.io, sign in, and type this into the text box: "Give me three simple ideas for a 10-minute daily habit that helps me [your goal, such as sleep better or save time]." Read the reply, then ask one follow-up question to improve it. You've just completed your first real conversation.
